case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, and under what circumstances, Sections 32(1)(a) and 43(a)(1)(A) of the Lanham Act allow trademark-infringement liability and remedies for a foreign defendant’s trademark “use in commerce” that occurs outside the United States.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Lanham Act §§ 32(1)(a) and 43(a)(1)(A), codified at 15 U.S.C. §§ 1114(1)(a) (registered-mark infringement) and 1125(a)(1)(A) (false designation of origin / unregistered marks), and the Supreme Court’s presumption against extraterritoriality framework (as articulated in RJR Nabisco).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Abitron) argue that the Lanham Act does not apply extraterritorially to foreign companies’ sales in foreign countries because Congress did not give an “affirmative and unmistakable” instruction to reach foreign conduct. They emphasize the traditional territorial nature of trademark law and contend that allowing U.S. Lanham Act claims based on foreign-market sales would improperly project U.S. trademark rules abroad. Under their approach, foreign uses/sales should fall outside §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) absent a clearly domestic use (and they seek reversal of liability and damages predicated on predominantly foreign conduct).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Hetronic) maintains that the Lanham Act can reach certain foreign trademark uses when they have sufficient U.S. connection—most importantly when the foreign conduct causes, or is likely to cause, confusion in U.S. commerce and harms a U.S. trademark owner’s goodwill and sales. Hetronic supports the Tenth Circuit’s general approach that focuses on U.S. effects (such as downstream U.S. sales, U.S. customer confusion, and harm to U.S. commerce), arguing that limiting the Act strictly to purely domestic “uses” would leave U.S. brand owners underprotected against modern cross-border infringement schemes.
key_precedents: RJR Nabisco, Inc. v. European Community, 579 U.S. 325 (2016)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s domestic-effects theory has intuitive force because the Lanham Act is consumer-protection legislation aimed at preventing confusion in U.S. commerce, and Steele v. Bulova recognizes that foreign misuse can “radiate” harm here. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, RJR Nabisco’s step-two focus inquiry must be anchored in the statute’s operative conduct, and §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) impose liability for the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce,” not for effects untethered to any domestic use—otherwise the presumption against extraterritoriality collapses into a general effects test. Bulova can be harmonized as fact-bound (substantial domestic ties and minimal conflict with foreign law), which is consistent with a narrow holding that the Act reaches only domestic “use in commerce,” with remedies limited accordingly. That approach best preserves comity and institutional legitimacy while leaving Congress room to speak clearly if it wants broader, effects-based coverage.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s domestic-effects theory—framing the Lanham Act’s “focus” as protecting U.S. consumers and goodwill—cannot displace the statute’s operative text, which imposes liability only for the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, RJR Nabisco step two requires us to locate that regulated conduct; treating downstream U.S. confusion as sufficient would collapse the presumption against extraterritoriality into a general effects test, contrary to Morrison and RJR Nabisco’s demand for a clear, affirmative congressional indication. Steele v. Bulova does not supply that indication; as Justice Alito and Justice Kagan explain, it is best read as fact-bound with substantial domestic anchors and limited comity conflict, not a license to regulate predominantly foreign sales by foreign defendants. Under a textualist and originalist approach, any broader reach based on domestic effects is for Congress to enact expressly, not for this Court to infer.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s domestic-effects framing is the best pushback, but it still treats U.S. confusion as the operative hook and thereby resurrects an effects test that Morrison and RJR Nabisco rejected absent a clear congressional statement. Under RJR Nabisco step two, the text of §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) makes the statute’s focus the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce,” not the downstream location of reputational injury, and Chief Justice Roberts is right that collapsing the inquiry into domestic effects would project U.S. trademark law into foreign markets with serious comity and administrability costs. Steele v. Bulova, as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan emphasize, is best harmonized as fact-bound with substantial domestic anchors and limited foreign-law conflict, not as a freestanding authorization for regulating predominantly foreign sales by foreign defendants. Tailoring remedies cannot cure an impermissibly extraterritorial application at the liability stage when the conduct Congress targeted—use in commerce—occurred abroad.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that RJR Nabisco step two requires identifying the statute’s “focus” from the text, and they argue §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) focus on the defendant’s “use in commerce,” not downstream effects, to avoid collapsing the presumption into a free-floating effects test. But I do not read “use in commerce” as a purely geographic locator; it is Congress’s jurisdictional hook aimed at protecting U.S. commerce—U.S. consumers and U.S. goodwill—from confusion and deception, so when foreign trademark use predictably and substantially causes domestic confusion or injury, applying the Act is not the kind of extraterritorial projection Morrison and RJR forbid. Steele v. Bulova Watch Co. supports that understanding by recognizing that foreign misuse can “radiate” consequences into the United States, and those domestic consequences can supply the necessary domestic application even if much of the conduct occurred abroad. The comity and administrability concerns Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kavanaugh raise can be handled through a demanding domestic-effects threshold and remedies limited to U.S.-tethered injury, rather than a categorical rule that immunizes schemes designed to exploit U.S. markets while externalizing the infringing “use” abroad.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s domestic-effects framing powerfully captures the Lanham Act’s consumer-protection aims, but under RJR Nabisco step two the question is what conduct the provisions make dispositive, and §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) key liability to the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce.” As the Chief Justice stresses, treating downstream U.S. confusion as the operative hook would effectively reintroduce an effects test with no clear limiting principle, undermining the presumption against extraterritoriality and creating comity friction by regulating foreign-market labeling and sales. Steele v. Bulova fits more coherently, as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett argue, as a fact-bound case with substantial domestic anchors and limited conflict, not a general authorization to reach predominantly foreign use. A conduct-centered, domestic-use rule remains the most textually grounded and administrable middle path, while leaving room to reach schemes with meaningful domestic sales, marketing, importation, or other domestic “use in commerce.”

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to emphasize the Lanham Act’s consumer-protection and goodwill purposes, and Bulova’s recognition that foreign misuse can “radiate” harm into the United States. But under RJR Nabisco step two, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas stress, the textual focus of §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) is the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce,” not downstream effects; adopting an effects-sufficient rule would effectively collapse the presumption against extraterritoriality whenever U.S. confusion is alleged. Bulova can be harmonized, as Justice Kagan notes, as fact-bound—substantial domestic ties and limited foreign-law conflict—without converting it into a general license to regulate predominantly foreign-market trademark use by foreign defendants. On a separation-of-powers and textualist view, any broader effects-based regime is for Congress to clearly authorize, while domestic use (including importation, U.S.-directed marketing, or U.S. sales) remains fully actionable.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that the Lanham Act serves consumer protection and U.S. goodwill, and Steele v. Bulova recognizes that foreign misuse can “radiate” domestic consequences. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, RJR Nabisco’s step-two “focus” inquiry must be grounded in the operative statutory conduct—here the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce”—and an effects-sufficient rule would collapse the presumption against extraterritoriality into a general domestic-injury test with serious comity and administrability costs. Steele can be harmonized, consistent with that framework, as turning on substantial domestic anchors (including the defendant’s U.S. connections) and limited foreign-law conflict, not as a clear congressional authorization to impose liability for predominantly foreign sales by foreign defendants. Tailored remedies can address genuinely domestic uses and importation, but damages keyed to foreign-market “use” remain impermissibly extraterritorial absent a clear statement from Congress.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s domestic-confusion framing is the strongest counterargument, but under RJR Nabisco step two the inquiry is what conduct the provisions regulate, and §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) make liability turn on the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce,” not on downstream injury alone. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, adopting an effects-based hook would collapse the presumption against extraterritoriality into a general effects test and invite significant comity frictions by effectively supervising foreign-market labeling and sales. Steele v. Bulova does not alter the analysis because, as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch argue, it is best read as fact-bound with substantial domestic anchors (and limited foreign-law conflict), not a clear, affirmative congressional instruction to reach predominantly foreign “use in commerce” by foreign defendants. Because Sotomayor’s approach cannot be reconciled with the textually identified focus without erasing the presumption’s limiting function, I remain with petitioner.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s domestic-effects framing remains the best case for the respondent because trademark law is meant to protect U.S. consumers and goodwill, and foreign misuse can predictably create real confusion at home. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuade me that RJR Nabisco step two requires locating the statute’s operative conduct—here, the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce”—and an effects-only theory risks collapsing the presumption against extraterritoriality into a generalized reputational-injury test. Steele v. Bulova, as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, can be harmonized as a fact-specific decision with substantial domestic anchors and limited comity conflict, rather than a broad authorization to police foreign-market sales by foreign defendants. As a pragmatic matter consistent with procedural fairness, a domestic-use tether is more administrable and avoids international friction while still leaving room for Congress to extend the Act expressly if it wishes.

John Roberts.reasoning: Applying the modern presumption against extraterritoriality under RJR Nabisco, §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) lack a clear, affirmative indication that Congress meant them to regulate foreign “use in commerce,” so liability must be limited to claims where the statute’s focus is domestic conduct. The Lanham Act’s focus is the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce” of the mark, not merely downstream foreign conduct that happens to produce some U.S. effects, and allowing damages keyed to predominantly foreign sales would risk projecting U.S. trademark law into other nations and undermine comity and institutional legitimacy. Steele v. Bulova Watch Co. can be understood as a narrow application where the relevant conduct and injury were sufficiently tied to the United States and did not create substantial foreign-law conflict, but it does not authorize a broad effects-based test untethered to domestic use. A restrained, domestically focused rule respects federalism and avoids sweeping extraterritorial remedies absent unmistakable congressional direction.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Sections 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) impose liability only for a defendant’s “use in commerce,” and nothing in their text supplies the “clear, affirmative indication” required to overcome the presumption against extraterritoriality. Under RJR Nabisco’s step two, the statute’s “focus” is the infringing “use in commerce,” so applying these provisions to uses that occur abroad is an extraterritorial application even if domestic confusion or downstream effects are alleged. Reading “commerce” (even as defined broadly in the Act) to encompass foreign-country sales would effectively nullify the presumption, contrary to Morrison and RJR Nabisco. Any broader, effects-based regime is a policy choice for Congress, not atextual judicial expansion of §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Applying RJR Nabisco’s two-step presumption against extraterritoriality, nothing in the text of Lanham Act §§ 32(1)(a) or 43(a)(1)(A), 15 U.S.C. §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A), contains a clear, affirmative indication that Congress meant to impose liability for a foreign defendant’s trademark “use in commerce” occurring abroad. At step two, the provisions’ focus is the defendant’s “use in commerce” of the mark (and related domestic commercial conduct), so predominantly foreign sales and foreign-market uses fall outside the statute even if they produce downstream effects in the United States. Steele v. Bulova Watch Co. is best read as a fact-bound application involving substantial domestic conduct and minimal foreign-law conflict, and it cannot displace the modern RJR Nabisco framework or justify an effects-only test that risks projecting U.S. trademark law into foreign markets. Limiting liability and remedies to domestic “use in commerce” also avoids serious practical and comity problems that would arise from U.S. courts policing foreign sales under U.S. standards.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Applying the presumption against extraterritoriality under RJR Nabisco, the Lanham Act’s “focus” in §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) is preventing misleading trademark use that causes confusion in U.S. commerce and harms U.S. goodwill, so the statute may permissibly reach foreign conduct when it produces substantial domestic confusion or injury. Steele v. Bulova Watch Co. supports liability where foreign infringement is not confined abroad and “radiate[s] unlawful consequences” into the United States, including diversion of U.S. sales and consumer confusion. A rigid rule limiting liability only to physically domestic “use” would underprotect U.S. mark owners against modern cross-border schemes and deny effective remedies where vulnerable consumers and smaller firms bear the brunt of deception. Consistent with fairness and pragmatic enforcement, remedies should be tailored to the domestic effects and to avoid unnecessary comity friction, but liability should not be categorically barred merely because the defendant is foreign and some sales occurred abroad.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Applying RJR Nabisco’s two-step framework, §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) contain no “affirmative and unmistakable” indication that Congress meant to regulate foreign trademark uses, so the presumption against extraterritoriality is not rebutted at step one. At step two, the provisions’ focus is the defendant’s “use in commerce” of the mark (and resulting confusion) in U.S. commerce; foreign sales and foreign uses, standing alone, are not domestic conduct merely because they have downstream U.S. effects. Steele v. Bulova Watch Co. can be reconciled as involving substantial domestic conduct and a weak comity case (including U.S.-citizen conduct and U.S.-based components), not as a free-floating effects test that would make the Lanham Act globally applicable whenever U.S. confusion is alleged. This narrower, conduct-centered rule is more workable and coherent, and it preserves room for liability where the infringing “use in commerce” is domestic even if parts of a scheme occur abroad.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Applying RJR Nabisco’s two-step framework, §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) contain no “affirmative and unmistakable” indication that Congress meant to regulate foreign trademark “use in commerce,” so the presumption against extraterritoriality is not rebutted at step one. At step two, the provisions’ focus is the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce” of the mark (and the statutorily defined “commerce” Congress can regulate), so liability and remedies may attach only when that use is domestic; downstream confusion or foreign sales’ effects in the United States, standing alone, cannot convert a foreign use into a domestic application. Steele v. Bulova Watch Co. can be reconciled as involving sufficient domestic conduct (including U.S.-based effects and the defendant’s U.S. connections), but it does not authorize a free-ranging effects test that projects U.S. trademark law onto predominantly foreign transactions. A clear domestic-use rule better respects the statute’s text, the territorial nature of trademark rights, and separation-of-powers limits on courts expanding federal law beyond what Congress enacted.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Applying RJR Nabisco’s presumption against extraterritoriality, §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) contain no clear, affirmative indication that Congress authorized liability for a foreign defendant’s purely foreign “use in commerce,” so the case turns on whether the application is nonetheless domestic at step two. The focus of these provisions is the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce,” and when that use (sales, labeling, and marketing) occurs abroad, imposing Lanham Act liability and remedies would project U.S. trademark law into foreign markets and create serious workability and comity problems. Steele v. Bulova Watch Co. is best read as a narrow, fact-specific application (including U.S. citizenship and substantial domestic connections) rather than a general authorization to regulate foreign commerce, and it should be harmonized with RJR Nabisco by limiting relief to genuinely domestic uses and domestic injury. Accordingly, liability and damages predicated on predominantly foreign conduct should be reversed or narrowed to domestic uses and effects.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying RJR Nabisco’s two-step framework, §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) contain no “affirmative and unmistakable” indication of extraterritorial reach, so any application must be domestically tethered. At step two, the provisions’ textual “focus” is the defendant’s “use in commerce” of a mark “in connection with” goods or services that is likely to cause confusion, meaning the conduct relevant to the statute’s focus must occur in the United States to avoid an extraterritorial application. Treating foreign sales as actionable merely because they have downstream U.S. effects would convert the presumption into an effects test and risk projecting U.S. trademark law abroad, contrary to RJR Nabisco’s conduct-based inquiry. Steele v. Bulova Watch Co. does not compel a broader rule here because it involved significant domestic conduct and a U.S. defendant, and thus does not supply the clear statutory instruction needed to reach foreign defendants’ foreign “use in commerce.”

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Applying RJR Nabisco’s two-step framework, §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) lack a clear, affirmative indication of extraterritorial reach, so the Lanham Act cannot be applied to impose liability for a foreign defendant’s purely foreign “use in commerce.” At step two, the statute’s focus is the defendant’s “use in commerce” of the mark, not downstream effects like confusion; thus, when the relevant use occurs outside the United States, imposing liability would be an impermissibly extraterritorial application. Steele v. Bulova Watch Co. is best read narrowly as involving substantial domestic conduct and U.S. citizenship, and it does not displace the modern presumption analysis or authorize sweeping regulation of foreign-market sales by foreign defendants. Limiting liability to domestic uses promotes procedural fairness, predictable rules, and reduces international friction while leaving Congress room to expand coverage expressly if needed.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, and under what circumstances, Sections 32(1)(a) and 43(a)(1)(A) of the Lanham Act provide a cause of action and remedies for trademark “use in commerce” that occurs outside the United States, particularly foreign defendants’ foreign sales.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Lanham Act § 32(1)(a), 15 U.S.C. § 1114(1)(a) (infringement of a registered mark), and Lanham Act § 43(a)(1)(A), 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(A) (false designation of origin/unfair competition), analyzed through the federal presumption against extraterritoriality (as articulated in cases like RJR Nabisco).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Abitron and related entities) argue that the Lanham Act does not apply extraterritorially to foreign companies’ sales in foreign countries because Congress did not give a clear, affirmative instruction to regulate foreign conduct; trademarks are traditionally territorial; and allowing U.S. trademark suits based on foreign-market transactions would improperly extend U.S. law abroad and conflict with the presumption against extraterritoriality.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Hetronic) contends that the Lanham Act can reach at least some foreign “uses” of a mark when those uses have substantial effects in U.S. commerce—e.g., where foreign sales or marketing cause consumer confusion in the United States, divert U.S. sales, harm U.S. goodwill, or otherwise impact U.S. commerce—so liability and remedies are appropriate when the infringement is sufficiently connected to, or felt within, the United States.
key_precedents: RJR Nabisco, Inc. v. European Community, 579 U.S. 325 (2016)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s most forceful point is that the Lanham Act exists to prevent confusion in U.S. commerce and protect domestic goodwill, so substantial domestic effects from foreign sales should be enough. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, RJR Nabisco’s step-two “focus” inquiry cannot be satisfied by purpose alone; §§1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) tie liability to the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce,” and letting downstream U.S. injury transform wholly foreign transactions into domestic applications collapses the presumption into an unbounded effects test with serious comity and administrability costs. Steele v. Bulova can be accommodated on narrow, fact-bound grounds—substantial U.S. connections and limited foreign-law conflict—without converting it into a general authorization to regulate foreign-market sales by foreign defendants. A minimalist domestic-use rule preserves the Act’s core and leaves any broader effects-based regime to Congress’s clear instruction.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “substantial domestic effects” proposal rests on the Lanham Act’s broad purpose, but under RJR Nabisco and Morrison purpose cannot substitute for the statute’s textual focus; §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) attach liability to the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce,” not to downstream injury wherever felt. Chief Justice Roberts is correct that converting “use in commerce” into a free-floating effects test would collapse step two into policy and invite precisely the comity and unpredictability the presumption against extraterritoriality is meant to avoid. Steele v. Bulova does not undermine this reading because it can be understood as involving substantial domestic anchors and limited foreign-law conflict; it cannot rewrite the statute to reach wholly foreign sales by foreign defendants absent a domestic use. If Congress wishes to regulate foreign-market transactions based solely on U.S. effects, it must say so clearly in the text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “substantial, specific U.S. effects” proposal is the best counter, but it still converts RJR Nabisco’s step-two “focus” inquiry into an effects test untethered from what §§1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) actually regulate: the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Lanham Act’s repeated linkage of liability to transactional use makes it unnatural to treat wholly foreign sales by foreign defendants as domestic applications merely because confusion or goodwill injury is later felt in the United States. Steele v. Bulova, as Justice Thomas notes, can be harmonized as resting on substantial domestic connections and limited comity conflict; it does not supply the clear congressional authorization needed to police foreign marketplaces based on downstream U.S. effects. Practically, adopting Sotomayor’s effects threshold would predictably invite sprawling worldwide trademark litigation and comity friction—precisely what the presumption against extraterritoriality is designed to avert absent a clear textual statement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s RJR Nabisco “focus” point is the strongest rejoinder: if we define the focus as the defendant’s “use in commerce,” an effects-based approach risks looking like an end-run around Morrison’s territorial discipline. But I do not read “use in commerce” as purely a geographic limiter; it is a jurisdictional/definitional hook tied to Congress’s power over commerce, and the provisions’ object is preventing consumer confusion and diversion of U.S. goodwill—harms that can be intentionally caused through foreign transactions that are concretely tethered to the U.S. market. Justice Kagan’s administrability and comity concerns are real, yet a categorical foreign-sale bar creates an enforcement gap where sophisticated infringers can target U.S. consumers and U.S. reputational interests from just across the border; a cabined “substantial, specific U.S. effects” requirement with remedy tailoring answers those concerns without turning the Lanham Act into a worldwide trademark code. Steele v. Bulova, while not a free-floating effects test, supports looking to practical U.S.-centered injury and enforceability to avoid leaving domestic consumers and smaller markholders without meaningful protection when the disruption is felt in U.S. commerce.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “substantial, specific U.S. effects” proposal most directly challenges my view because it tries to honor the Lanham Act’s consumer-protection aims while cabining comity and administrability through tailored remedies. But under RJR Nabisco’s step-two focus inquiry, I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) regulate the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce,” and treating downstream domestic confusion as sufficient effectively turns focus into purpose and collapses the presumption into a generalized effects test. Steele v. Bulova, as Justice Alito and Justice Barrett note, fits better as a narrow case with substantial U.S. anchors and limited foreign-law conflict, not as authorization to reach wholly foreign sales by foreign defendants whenever U.S. goodwill is impacted. A domestic-use rule remains the most textually coherent and workable line while still covering importation, U.S.-directed marketing, and other genuinely domestic conduct that creates consumer confusion here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point remains that the Lanham Act seeks to protect U.S. commerce and goodwill, so a “substantial domestic effects” rule might better serve the statute’s aims. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, RJR Nabisco step two asks what the particular provisions regulate, and §§1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) attach liability to the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce,” not to downstream injury wherever it is felt; an effects-only trigger would effectively smuggle in the clear statement the presumption requires. Steele v. Bulova can still be honored on narrow, fact-bound grounds—substantial domestic anchors and limited comity conflict—as Justice Thomas notes, without converting it into a license to treat wholly foreign sales as domestic applications. Without domestic use (importation, U.S.-directed marketing, U.S. point-of-sale activity), applying the Act to foreign-market transactions is extraterritorial, and it is for Congress, not us, to extend the statute further.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that foreign sales can substantially harm U.S. consumers and domestic goodwill, and she proposes a “substantial, specific U.S. effects” test with tailored remedies. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, RJR Nabisco requires us to identify the provisions’ “focus,” and §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) attach liability to the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce,” not to downstream injury untethered to a domestic transaction; an effects-only trigger would effectively supply the clear extraterritorial statement Congress did not provide. Steele v. Bulova can be accommodated on its facts (strong U.S. connections and sensitivity to foreign-law conflict) without converting it into a general license for U.S. courts to police foreign-market sales, which would raise serious comity and administrability concerns. The Act still reaches domestic anchors—imports, U.S.-directed marketing, and U.S. point-of-sale uses—so the feared enforcement gap does not justify rewriting the statute’s territorial reach.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that the Lanham Act’s protective purpose—shielding U.S. commerce and goodwill from confusion—would be undercut if foreign sales producing substantial U.S. injury escape liability. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, RJR Nabisco’s step-two “focus” inquiry is tethered to the conduct Congress regulated in §§1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A): the defendant’s actionable “use in commerce,” not downstream effects untethered to a domestic use. An effects-only trigger would effectively supply the clear statement missing at step one and invite the comity and administrability concerns Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch identify, by converting foreign-market disputes into domestic cases whenever a plaintiff alleges U.S. confusion. Steele v. Bulova can be accommodated on the narrower reading Roberts and Thomas describe—substantial domestic anchors and limited foreign-law conflict—without turning it into a general authorization to police wholly foreign sales by foreign defendants.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “substantial, specific U.S. effects” proposal powerfully foregrounds the Lanham Act’s consumer-protection purpose and the risk of an enforcement gap, but under RJR Nabisco that policy concern cannot displace the step-two focus inquiry. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan stress, §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) attach liability to the defendant’s infringing “use in commerce,” and treating foreign-market sales as domestic applications whenever a plaintiff alleges U.S. injury would collapse the presumption into an effects test with serious comity and administrability costs. Steele v. Bulova still matters, but I agree with Justice Barrett that it is best read as a fact-bound case with concrete domestic anchors and attention to foreign-law conflict, not a license to reach wholly foreign sales by foreign defendants. On a progressive-pragmatist view, that domestic-use rule is also more procedurally fair and predictable, while leaving room for tailored remedies when the defendant’s conduct is genuinely U.S.-directed (imports, U.S. advertising, or domestic point-of-sale).

John Roberts.reasoning: Applying RJR Nabisco’s two-step presumption against extraterritoriality, §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) lack a clear, affirmative indication that Congress meant to regulate wholly foreign “use in commerce,” particularly foreign defendants’ foreign sales. At step two, the “focus” of these provisions is domestic use in commerce that creates actionable confusion in U.S. commerce; foreign transactions that occur abroad, even if they have downstream effects, are not themselves the statute’s focus absent domestic use or other domestic conduct. Steele v. Bulova Watch Co. is best read narrowly—as permitting relief where substantial domestic connections exist (including the defendant’s U.S. citizenship and effects on U.S. commerce)—and does not overcome the modern presumption framework to authorize a broad effects-only test for foreign sales by foreign defendants. A narrow, domestic-use limitation better respects federalism and international comity while preserving the Act’s core function and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Sections 32(1)(a) and 43(a)(1)(A) impose liability for “use in commerce,” and nothing in 15 U.S.C. §§ 1114(1)(a) or 1125(a)(1)(A) contains the clear, affirmative indication required to regulate wholly foreign sales by foreign defendants, so the presumption against extraterritoriality controls. Under RJR Nabisco, Inc. v. European Community, the Court must identify the statute’s “focus,” and here the focus is the infringing “use in commerce” that causes confusion—conduct that, when occurring abroad as foreign sales, is not transformed into domestic application merely because it has downstream effects in the United States. Steele v. Bulova Watch Co. does not supply a general “effects” test untethered to text; at most it reflects an application involving significant domestic contacts (including the defendant’s U.S. citizenship and domestic effects) and cannot overcome the modern presumption analysis. Consistent with limited federal power and respect for territorial sovereignty, the Act should reach only domestic “use in commerce” (e.g., direct sales or marketing into the United States), not purely foreign transactions.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Applying RJR Nabisco’s two-step presumption against extraterritoriality, neither Lanham Act §32(1)(a), 15 U.S.C. §1114(1)(a), nor §43(a)(1)(A), 15 U.S.C. §1125(a)(1)(A), contains a clear, affirmative indication that Congress meant to regulate foreign defendants’ purely foreign sales. At step two, the provisions’ domestic “focus” is best understood as the defendant’s “use in commerce” (i.e., the transactional use/sale of goods under the mark), consistent with the Act’s structure tying trademark rights and maintenance to domestic “use in commerce” (see 15 U.S.C. §§1051(a), 1058(b)), rather than an amorphous “effects” test keyed to downstream confusion. Treating foreign-market transactions as actionable whenever they have U.S. effects would invite substantial interference with other nations’ regulation of their own markets and produce unpredictable, expansive liability—practical consequences this Court has warned against in Morrison and RJR Nabisco. Therefore, foreign defendants’ foreign sales are not reachable absent a domestic use in commerce, even if the plaintiff alleges some domestic harm.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Applying the presumption against extraterritoriality as articulated in RJR Nabisco, the relevant focus of Lanham Act §§ 32(1)(a) and 43(a)(1)(A) is the protection of U.S. commerce from consumer confusion and diversion of goodwill, so a claim may proceed where foreign “uses in commerce” have substantial, concrete effects in U.S. commerce. Steele v. Bulova Watch Co. confirms that, in appropriate circumstances, the Lanham Act can reach foreign conduct—particularly when the infringement foreseeably harms U.S. consumers or the U.S. markholder’s domestic goodwill—and remedies should be tailored to redress that U.S.-centered injury. A categorical bar on liability for foreign sales by foreign defendants would create a practical enforcement gap that disproportionately harms smaller businesses and consumers unable to police cross-border confusion. Consistent with the Act’s remedial purposes, courts should permit relief when the plaintiff proves a strong nexus to U.S. commerce (e.g., confusion in the United States, diversion of U.S. sales, or harm to U.S. goodwill), while avoiding orders that unnecessarily regulate purely foreign disputes.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Applying RJR Nabisco’s two-step framework, Sections 32(1)(a) and 43(a)(1)(A) lack a clear, affirmative indication that Congress meant to regulate purely foreign “use in commerce,” so the presumption against extraterritoriality is not rebutted at step one. At step two, the statute’s focus is domestic—protecting U.S. trademark rights and preventing consumer confusion in U.S. commerce—so liability should attach only when the infringing “use in commerce” is domestic, not when foreign defendants make foreign sales abroad. Steele v. Bulova Watch Co. can be read consistently with that approach because it involved substantial U.S.-centered ties and confusion, and it cautioned against overreach where foreign sovereignty and conflict concerns are present. A domestic-use rule is more workable and predictable than open-ended “effects” tests, while still allowing remedies when the relevant use (e.g., sales, marketing, or distribution) occurs in the United States.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Applying RJR Nabisco’s two-step framework, neither § 32(1)(a) nor § 43(a)(1)(A) contains a clear, affirmative indication of extraterritorial application, so the presumption against extraterritoriality is not rebutted. At step two, the statute’s focus is on the defendant’s “use in commerce” of the mark in a way that causes confusion—language that, read in its ordinary sense and against the Act’s territorial background, targets domestic commercial use rather than foreign sales consummated abroad. Permitting liability and remedies keyed to foreign defendants’ foreign transactions based on downstream effects in the United States would risk international discord and effectively rewrite the statute’s territorial limits, a move better left to Congress. Where the complained-of “use in commerce” is domestic (e.g., U.S. sales, marketing, or importation), the Act applies; but foreign sales abroad, standing alone, do not supply a domestic application.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Applying the modern presumption against extraterritoriality under RJR Nabisco, §§ 32(1)(a) and 43(a)(1)(A) contain no clear, affirmative indication that Congress authorized liability for a foreign defendant’s foreign “use in commerce,” including foreign sales. At step two, the Lanham Act’s focus is on domestic “use in commerce” and domestic confusion/marketplace effects in U.S. commerce, so imposing liability and remedies based on purely foreign transactions is an impermissible extraterritorial application. Steele v. Bulova Watch Co. is best understood as a case where the relevant conduct and effects implicated U.S. commerce and did not create substantial conflict with foreign law, not as a blanket “effects” test authorizing global regulation. A rule limiting the cause of action to domestic uses is more workable, respects territoriality and comity concerns, and avoids turning U.S. trademark law into a worldwide code absent clear congressional instruction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying RJR Nabisco’s two-step framework, Sections 32(1)(a) and 43(a)(1)(A) contain no clear, affirmative indication of extraterritorial application; the phrase “use in commerce” in 15 U.S.C. §§ 1114(1)(a) and 1125(a)(1)(A) is a jurisdictional hook tied to Congress’s Commerce Clause power, not an instruction to regulate foreign-market sales. At step two, the provisions’ focus is the defendant’s actionable “use in commerce” of the mark (i.e., the infringing use tied to regulated commerce), so applying the Act to wholly foreign sales by foreign defendants is impermissibly extraterritorial absent a domestic use. Precedent reinforces that when the presumption is unrebutted, courts may not extend liability and remedies to foreign conduct simply because domestic effects are alleged. Any broader “effects” test would risk methodological inconsistency with RJR Nabisco and invite international friction contrary to the presumption’s purposes.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Applying the presumption against extraterritoriality as articulated in RJR Nabisco, Inc. v. European Community, §§ 32(1)(a) and 43(a)(1)(A) lack a clear, affirmative indication that Congress intended to impose liability based on purely foreign “use in commerce,” such as foreign defendants’ foreign sales. At step two, the provisions’ focus is domestic—protecting U.S. trademark rights and U.S. commerce from infringing uses—and extending liability to foreign-market transactions risks unpredictable, potentially sweeping remedies untethered to domestic conduct, with serious comity and administrability consequences. Steele v. Bulova Watch Co. confirms the Act can apply in appropriate circumstances, but it does not justify treating foreign sales alone as actionable absent a concrete domestic use (e.g., importation or U.S.-directed sales/marketing) that makes the case domestic in its statutory focus. Consistent with procedural fairness and practical consequences, limiting liability and remedies to domestic uses provides a clearer rule and avoids converting effects abroad into a roving mandate to police global trademark disputes from U.S. courts.
